title: Prairie iGaming 2026: Saskatchewan and Manitoba Explained
excerpt: Saskatchewan and Manitoba both run online gambling through PlayNow.com. Here is how the single-operator Prairie model works in 2026 and what could change next.
author: Lisa Davids
bodyHtml:
Canada's iGaming map has been redrawn twice in four years: first by Ontario in 2022, then by Alberta in July 2026. Both moves drew enormous attention, and both involved opening the doors to private operators. Online gambling in Saskatchewan and Manitoba has taken the opposite path. On the Prairies, the province remains the only legal online gambling provider, and in both cases that provider runs on the same underlying platform, PlayNow.com.

That makes the two provinces a useful counterpoint to the competitive markets on either side of them. Both have concluded, so far, that a single publicly accountable operator serves residents better than a licensed field of private brands. Here is how the model actually works in 2026, what it means in practice, and what might realistically change.

How the Prairie model works

Manitoba

Manitoba Liquor & Lotteries, the provincial Crown corporation, offers legal online gambling through PlayNow.com. Crucially, it did not build the platform itself. Manitoba entered a partnership with the British Columbia Lottery Corporation, which developed and operates PlayNow, and licensed that technology for Manitoba players rather than duplicating the cost of a bespoke system. Manitoba was the first province outside British Columbia to take that route, and the arrangement has been in place for well over a decade. The practical result is a site that looks and behaves much like the BC version, with a Manitoba front end, Manitoba-specific lottery products, and revenue that returns to the province rather than to private shareholders.

Saskatchewan

Saskatchewan came to regulated online gambling considerably later, launching its own PlayNow.com in 2022. The structure is what makes it distinctive. Rather than a straightforward Crown monopoly, Saskatchewan's online platform is the product of an agreement between the province and the Saskatchewan Indian Gaming Authority, the First Nations organisation that operates the province's land-based casinos. SIGA runs the online business, the provincial regulator oversees it, and the technology again comes from BCLC.

That is not a cosmetic distinction. It means Saskatchewan's single-operator model rests on a revenue-sharing relationship with First Nations, and any future decision to license private competitors would have to be negotiated within that framework rather than imposed over it. Anyone predicting a quick pivot to an Ontario-style market in Saskatchewan is probably underestimating how much sits behind the current arrangement.

What a single-operator market means for players

The trade-offs of a monopoly model are fairly consistent wherever you find them, and the Prairies are no exception. Players get a strong floor and a lower ceiling.

  • Accountability is clear. One operator, one regulator, one province. If something goes wrong with your account, there is a domestic body ultimately answerable for it.
  • Marketing is restrained. There is no bidding war for your deposit, which means far less advertising pressure than Ontario residents have experienced.
  • Promotions are modest. Without competitors, there is little reason to offer aggressive welcome bonuses, and Prairie players will find the offers considerably smaller than those advertised elsewhere.
  • Game libraries are narrower. A provincial platform curates a selection rather than aggregating everything on the market, so the slot and live dealer catalogues are smaller than a large private operator's.
  • Money stays in the province. Net revenue supports provincial programs, and in Saskatchewan's case flows through the First Nations gaming framework as well.

None of that is inherently better or worse than the alternative. It is a different set of priorities, weighted toward control and public return rather than choice and price competition.

How online gambling in Saskatchewan and Manitoba compares with Ontario and Alberta

Ontario's competitive market has now run for four years. It brought dozens of private operators under provincial regulation, produced a large tax base, and created genuine competition on odds, promotions and product depth. It also generated advertising saturation significant enough that the province tightened rules on celebrity and athlete endorsements. Our guide to Ontario sports betting covers how that market has settled. Alberta launched its own competitive market in July 2026, with the advantage of having watched Ontario before writing its rules, and we track it in our Alberta sports betting coverage. Early commentary there has been cautiously positive, though a market that young cannot yet tell you much about long-term outcomes on either revenue or player harm.

Set against those two, the Prairie provinces look conservative but coherent. A Saskatchewan or Manitoba player has one legal option instead of dozens. That option is safe, locally accountable and reasonably well featured, but it will not match a competitive market on breadth, bonus value or the pace at which new products appear. The honest summary is that the monopoly model delivers a better regulatory guarantee and a weaker consumer proposition.

The grey-market question

A monopoly on licensing is not a monopoly on player behaviour, and this is where the Prairie model runs into its central difficulty.

Internationally licensed operators accept customers from Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and many residents use them. Canadian law targets the operation of unlicensed gambling within a province rather than the individual who places a bet, so players are not the ones exposed to prosecution. Practically speaking, these sites operate in a grey zone: not provincially licensed, not meaningfully blocked, and not going anywhere.

Estimates of how much money leaves the Prairies this way circulate frequently, but most originate with parties who have a commercial interest in the answer, and specific figures deserve caution. What is not really disputed is the direction: when one regulated platform competes against a global field with larger libraries and bigger promotions, a meaningful share of players will use the alternatives. That was precisely the argument Ontario made when it opened its market, and the one Alberta echoed.

If you do play at an internationally licensed site, the licensing jurisdiction is the single most useful signal of how much recourse you would actually have, and it deserves more attention than the size of the welcome offer.

Protections, tools and dispute resolution

The strongest argument for the Prairie model is what happens when something goes wrong. On a provincial platform, identity and age verification are mandatory, funds sit with a Crown-backed or provincially supervised operator, and complaints have a clear escalation path within the province. Responsible gambling tooling is built into the account rather than bolted on: deposit limits, time limits, self-assessment tools, self-exclusion and links to provincial problem-gambling services. In Saskatchewan, responsible gaming programming has been a visible priority for SIGA across both its land-based and online operations.

Offshore sites vary enormously on all of this. Some licensing bodies run credible complaints processes; others exist mainly on paper. The gap is not that offshore operators are uniformly bad, but that quality is inconsistent and the burden of checking falls entirely on you.

Product range: sports, casino and poker

Both Prairie PlayNow sites cover the three main verticals. Single-event sports betting has been legal across Canada since 2021, and both provinces offer it alongside parlays and live in-play markets, with strong coverage of the NHL, NFL, CFL and major soccer. The casino side carries slots, table games and live dealer content from established studios, though the catalogue is curated rather than exhaustive. Our overview of online casino games in Canada explains what to look for when comparing libraries.

Poker is the weakest link, as it is for most provincial platforms. Liquidity is the constraint: a player pool drawn from one province cannot sustain the traffic, game variety or tournament schedules that international networks offer. Interprovincial pooling would help, but it requires agreements that do not currently exist at scale in Canada.

What might come next

The realistic near-term expectation for both provinces is continuity. Neither government has announced a move toward competitive licensing, and neither faces the immediate pressure that pushed Ontario and Alberta.

Two things could shift that. The first is the Alberta demonstration effect. If Alberta's market shows over the next few years that competitive licensing increases regulated participation without worsening harm indicators, the case for a monopoly becomes harder to argue on player-protection grounds alone. If the data goes the other way, Prairie caution will look well judged. It is genuinely too early to say which. The second is fiscal. Licensing revenue is one of the few levers that raises money without a new tax on residents. Set against it is scale: Saskatchewan and Manitoba are relatively small markets, and a licensed field only works if enough operators find entry worth the compliance cost.

Saskatchewan carries the additional dimension of First Nations gaming rights, which have shaped policy in the province for decades. Any expansion there would need to preserve, not dilute, the position SIGA currently holds, which points toward a negotiated or hybrid outcome rather than a straight copy of Alberta, if change comes at all. We follow provincial developments as they happen in our gambling news section.

The bottom line

The Prairies in 2026 represent the middle of Canada's iGaming spectrum in more than a geographic sense. Manitoba and Saskatchewan offer a legal, well-protected, locally accountable option that is deliberately modest in scope, while a much larger and less accountable market operates alongside it without formal provincial sanction. Players choosing between the two are really choosing between recourse and range.

Whether that balance holds will depend less on anything happening in Regina or Winnipeg than on what the numbers out of Edmonton look like in two or three years.

You must be 19+ (18+ in some provinces) to gamble in Canada. If gambling stops being fun, free confidential help is available in every province.
